sentences.text: Bothriolepis is characterized by bony plates covering its head and the anterior part of its trunk, featuring a keyhole-shaped opening on the top for eyes and nostrils and a mouth opening on the lower side near the front.
In adults, the animal possessed two separate jaw halves that were functionally independent, along with a single high, rounded posterior dorsal fin.

Its slender trunk was likely covered in soft skin without scales or markings, while the gill region was positioned more dorsally, anteriorly crowded, and relatively short and broad compared to normal fish.
The head and trunk armor of the species B. africana ranged from 20 to 300 mm, corresponding to full body lengths between 52 and 780 mm.
More than two hundred individuals of Bothriolepis were found packed closely together at the Catskill Formation site.
This creature possessed a specialized complex spiral valve in its digestive system, similar to that found in some sharks.
Bothriolepis is the most diverse genus of placoderms, with over 100 species found on all continents.
The genus Bothriolepis was described by Eichwald in 1840.
The species Bothriolepis canadensis was first described in 1880 by J.F. Whiteaves.
B. coloradensis was first described by Eastman in 1904 and found in present-day Colorado.
Remains of B. africana have been recovered exclusively from the Witpoort Formation near Makhanda/Grahamstown in South Africa.
Bothriolepis rex was originally described by Downs et al. in 2016 from the Nordstrand Point Formation of Ellesmere Island, Canada.
Most species of Bothriolepis were small, benthic freshwater detritivores averaging about 30 cm in length, with the ventral positioning of the mouth suggesting it was a bottom-feeder.
The animal fed by swallowing mouthfuls of mud and soft sediments to digest detritus, microorganisms, algae, and organic matter.
Researchers suggest Bothriolepis used its spike-like pectoral fins to lift its armored body off the bottom.
Downs et al. (2016) suggest that the thick armor of Bothriolepis rex served to protect against predators and acted as ballast to prevent the large bottom-dweller from floating.
Robert Denison published a paper exploring the soft anatomy and organs of Bothriolepis.
Bothriolepis is classified within the class Placodermi, the order Antiarchi, and the family Bothriolepidae.

Bothriolepis lived during the Late Middle Devonian, approximately 387 to 360 million years ago, with the time range extending from the Emsian to the Famennian stages, between 410.62 and 358.86 million years ago.
It inhabited near-shore marine and freshwater environments across all paleocontinents, with fossils found in Asia, Europe, Australia, Africa, North America, and South America.
It is unclear exactly when gnathostomes emerged, though the fossil record suggests the Early Palaeozoic era.
It is debated whether Bothriolepis had a notochord, as the trunk outline suggests one but no direct evidence exists due to soft tissue decay.
It is debated whether the ventral sacs of Bothriolepis functioned as lungs that allowed the animal to travel on land.
It is debated whether B. coloradensis is similar to or identical to B. nitida due to the fragmented nature of the available material.
There is significant debate regarding whether B. nitida and B. virginiensis can be distinguished from one another.
